newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British manufacturing emerges from doldrums.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British manufacturing emerges from doldrums.

text.p: British manufacturing, until now the weak spot in the country's economic recovery, emerged from the doldrums in August, according to an authoritative business survey published on Monday.
The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said both output and new orders expanded more rapidly last month than at any time since the spring of 1995.
Its Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) rose to a seasonally adjusted 51.8 percent in August, its highest level for a year, from 51.0 percent in July.
"This suggests that the slowdown in manufacturing activity, which began in late 1994, probably bottomed out in May," the CIPS said.
"Since then, rising consumers' expenditure has been the main driving force behind steadily accelerating growth in the manufacturing sector."
The survey showed prices slightly higher, but still at a low level historically, while employment remained flat.
The Conservative government, which faces a general election within the next nine months, said the figures showed the prospects for manufacturing had brightened.

But economists said the survey, based on a questionnaire sent to 310 industrial companies, would make it more difficult for Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke to cut interest rates again.
Clarke has cut official interest rates four times since December to their present 5.75 percent level.
With the Conservatives trailing well behind the opposition Labour party in opinion polls, he has a strong political incentive to do so again, despite opposition from the Bank of England.

Ciaran Barr, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the survey reinforced the Bank of England's argument that the economy was starting to turn around and did not need the stimulus of another interest rate cut.
"The PMI survey is very encouraging indeed," he said.
"We are finally seeing signs that the pickup in consumer activity is feeding right the way through the economy, with production of intermediate goods up, orders up and output up."
However, other economists cautioned that the improvement in manufacturing was far from dramatic.
"The survey shows manufacturing off its knees, but it's sluggish," said Michael Dicks of Lehman Brothers.
The Bank of England said M0, its narrow measure of money supply, rose a seasonally adjusted 7.5 percent in the year to August, up from 7.1 percent in July and above financial market expectations.
Economists said this was further evidence of buoyant consumer spending and would provide fresh ammunition for the central bank to argue that another rate cut was not be justified.

"M0 has recently tended to be dismissed by the Treasury as an indicator of nominal spending, but over the years it has proved more reliable than any other indicator at predicting future inflation trends," said Andrew Cates of stockbrokers UBS.
